title: the great departure
hookLine: the kingdom is handed on, the brothers and Draupadi take off their ornaments and walk out of the city, and a dog follows them
carry: vanaprastha: hand it on, give it back
tomorrow: someone falls in the sea of sand. why doesn't Yudhishthira turn around?

lines: SIX WALK OUT, AND A DOG.
cards: The news from Dwaraka reaches Hastinapura: Krishna is gone, and his clan has destroyed itself. Yudhishthira makes up his mind in one sentence, in Ganguli's telling: time is cooking all creatures. It's time to go.
He crowns Parikshit, the child who was born without breath, now grown, and puts the kingdom in others' care.
Then the five brothers and Draupadi take off their jewelry, put on the plain clothes of forest hermits, and walk out through the gates. The city follows a little way, weeping, and turns back.
One companion does not turn back. A dog.

teach.b: This is the Mahaprasthanika, the book of the great departure. The Pandavas walk east first: Yudhishthira leads, then Bhima, Arjuna, the twins, Draupadi, and the dog behind them all.
They reach the sea, and a figure stands in their path, tall as a mountain: Agni, the god of fire. He speaks to Arjuna. Remember the great bow Gandiva?
Agni brought it to Arjuna long ago, from Varuna, lord of the waters. Its work is finished; it belongs to Varuna; give it back.

teach.h: THE BOW GOES INTO THE WAVES
teach.b: And Arjuna, who carried it through the whole war, throws it into the waves and walks on unarmed. Here's the teaching.
Hindu tradition maps a life in four stages: the student, the householder, then vanaprastha, the forest-dweller who hands the household on, and sannyasa, the renouncer who sets everything down.

teach.h: VANAPRASTHA: HAND IT ON, GIVE IT BACK
teach.b: Many teachers read this morning as those last stages acted out: the kingdom to Parikshit, the jewels off at the gate, the bow back to the god it came from.

The Isha Upanishad opens the same way: all this belongs to the Lord, so enjoy it by letting it go. That's why many Hindu elders still hand on jewelry, duties and the family puja, and set out on pilgrimage.
Not as an ending. As the next stage. Then they walk on around the edge of the world, toward Meru.

how: The Mahaprasthanika Parva tells the Pandavas' final walk; Hindus hear it in recitations of the epic, and the image of the brothers, Draupadi and the dog walking toward the Himalayas is often painted and retold.

games.q: you're Arjuna, at the edge of the sea. the god of fire asks you to give back the bow that has made you who you are. what do you do?
o: keep it; you may still need it.
games.why: Arjuna throws Gandiva and his quivers into the water, returning them to Varuna, and walks on. idam na mama: it was never only his.

practice: Let your hands rest open and bring to mind one thing you're known for, a skill, a role, a title. When Hindus make offerings into a sacred fire, each one is often followed by the words idam na mama: this is not mine.
Breathe in and thank your gift for its work; breathe out and say silently, idam na mama, and notice what's left when it's not in your grip. If you don't pray, just say: this was never only mine.
